The story is told entirely from the single, retrospective first-person perspective of Tess. Furthermore, there are no truly "unlikeable," morally ambiguous, or repugnant characters in the narrative whose mindsets are explored. The closest is Tess's mother, who is initially depicted as somewhat cold and proud regarding the divorce, yet she is still shown to be compassionate and supportive when it matters (allowing Tess to go on the cruise, telling her to "be good to him," and holding Daniel's hand on his deathbed). The story focuses on warmth, belonging, and grief within a loving community rather than diving into the motivations of difficult or objectionable characters.
